overview.title: Oxidation Process
content: A process of growing a protective silicon dioxide (SiO₂) layer on the silicon wafer surface by reacting it with oxygen (O₂) or water vapor (H₂O) at high temperatures (800~1200°C).

The grown oxide layer plays crucial roles in semiconductor manufacturing, such as acting as an insulating layer to prevent leakage current, a diffusion barrier during ion implantation, and a hard mask during etching.

components.name: Furnace
components.desc: A quartz tube type equipment that heats the wafers to high temperatures.

components.name: Heater
components.desc: Precisely controls and maintains the temperature inside the furnace between 800°C and 1200°C.

components.name: Gas Inlet
components.desc: Injects the necessary O₂ gas or water vapor for the oxidation reaction.

components.name: Wafer Boat
components.desc: A quartz structure that holds tens to hundreds of wafers vertically.

principle.title: Operating Principle (Deal-Grove Model)
content: Oxide growth is explained by two mechanisms where oxygen molecules diffuse through the existing oxide layer and react at the silicon surface. This is known as the Deal-Grove Model.
1. Linear Growth Regime: Occurs when the initial oxide is thin, and the growth is determined by the chemical reaction rate at the surface.
2. Parabolic Growth Regime: As the oxide thickens, it takes longer for oxygen molecules to diffuse, gradually slowing down the growth rate.

test.question: Which process has a faster oxide growth rate: Dry Oxidation or Wet Oxidation?
options: Both processes have the same rate.
It depends on the temperature, but usually dry is faster.
test.explanation: Wet oxidation has a much faster growth rate because the water molecules (H₂O) used diffuse through the silicon oxide layer much faster than oxygen molecules (O₂).

theory.title: 2. Oxidation Process Advanced Theory
content: The oxidation process is a thermodynamic process that forms a thin and uniform silicon dioxide (SiO2) layer on the surface of a silicon (Si) wafer by reacting oxygen (O2) or water vapor (H2O).

This oxide layer acts as an excellent insulator and plays an indispensable role in semiconductor manufacturing, such as the gate oxide of transistors, a diffusion barrier mask during ion implantation, and isolation between devices.

The most widely used physical model is the Deal-Grove model. This model mathematically defines the growth rate of the oxide layer through the continuity of three fluxes: 1) movement of oxygen molecules from the gas region to the oxide surface, 2) diffusion through the previously formed oxide layer, and 3) a chemical reaction (Si + O2 -> SiO2) at the silicon-oxide interface.

Dry Oxidation uses pure oxygen gas, which has a slow growth rate but forms a dense film with excellent electrical properties. It is mainly used where a thin and high-quality layer is required, such as a gate oxide.
Wet Oxidation utilizes water vapor, resulting in a very fast growth rate. It is mainly used to form thick protective layers or isolation layers.
